state.case_summary:
A 51-year-old male with end-stage renal failure due to biopsy-confirmed IgA nephritis began hemodialysis in April 1977. He received cadaveric kidney transplants in 1980, 1985, and 1997. In 1998, he underwent parathyroidectomy for severe tertiary hyperparathyroidism. From 1997 to November 2003, he did not require dialysis. Hemodialysis was resumed in December 2003 due to declining kidney function, and a transplant biopsy indicated chronic transplant vasculopathy. The graft was left in place to maintain residual diuresis. His immunosuppressive regimen was reduced to 5 mg prednisone and 50 mg azathioprine daily until October 2004, after which only 5 mg prednisone was administered daily. In June 2005, the patient exhibited an inflammatory syndrome with a slightly elevated body temperature (up to 37.5°C) and general weakness. A subsequent transplant biopsy revealed tubulointerstitial nephritis in addition to the known transplant vasculopathy. The graft was removed at the end of June 2005, and immunosuppression was completely withdrawn. A few days later, the patient experienced a moderate fever and testicular pain. Ultrasound imaging suggested epididymitis. Empiric treatment with ciprofloxacin did not alleviate the symptoms or the ultrasound findings of the enlarged epididymis. Over the following weeks, the patient's condition worsened, with complaints of insomnia, severe pruritus, and an unintended weight loss of 4 kg over 12 weeks. Alternating arthralgia was a significant symptom. X-rays and ultrasound examinations of the affected joints did not indicate specific bone conditions. Laboratory tests revealed a rapidly increasing serum calcium level of 2.84 mmol/l (normal range: 2.2–2.65 mmol/l), despite normal or slightly elevated serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels (PTH intact: 1.2–4.5 pmol/l). Serum alkaline phosphatase was elevated at 173 U/l (normal range: 35–104 U/l). C-reactive protein was moderately elevated. The patient was switched to a low calcium dialysate concentration and the phosphate binder sevelamer. Vitamin D supplementation had been discontinued more than three months prior. Despite these interventions, the high serum calcium level and clinical symptoms persisted.

X-rays of the thorax revealed a pathological hilus configuration. A thoracic CT scan showed mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathia of 2–3 cm in diameter and a disseminated, micronodulary shaped densities of both lungs. Broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL) revealed a CD4/CD8 ratio above the normal value. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level: 158 U/l (normal value: 20–60 U/l). Soluble Interleukin2 receptor: 4133 U/ml (normal value: 220–710 U/ml) were elevated.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

root.label: Subacute Progressive Multisystem Syndrome with Hypercalcaemia, Lymphadenopathy, and Pulmonary Involvement
supporting_facts: Recurring kidney transplants and chronic transplant vasculopathy
Recent graft removal and cessation of immunosuppression
Rapidly increasing serum calcium level despite normal PTH levels
Elevated alkaline phosphatase and C-reactive protein
Lymphadenopathy and micronodular lung densities on thoracic CT scan
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme and soluble Interleukin-2 receptor levels
excluded_candidates: Primary hyperparathyroidism: normal PTH levels despite hypercalcaemia
Malignancy: no clear evidence of cancer, but lymphadenopathy and hypercalcaemia raise suspicion
Sarcoidosis: elevated ACE level and lymphadenopathy, but other findings do not strongly support this diagnosis
